edits.old: Dropping an index merely because one node reports zero accesses can make a capacity reduction unsafe. MongoDB documents node-local usage counters and testing with hidden indexes; Percona also warns to check application hints before removing indexes. (high confidence)
edits.new: Dropping an index merely because one node reports zero accesses can make a capacity reduction unsafe. MongoDB documents that $indexStats reports usage only for the node where the query runs (so run it on each node) and recommends hiding indexes to evaluate their impact before dropping them. Percona notes that the ops counter is reset when mongod restarts, so a zero count means unused only since the index was added or the server restarted. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/data-modeling/design-antipatterns/unnecessary-indexes/ ; https://www.percona.com/blog/identifying-unused-indexes-in-mongodb/

edits.old: Self-managed container sizing must respect the container memory limit and leave room beyond WiredTiger cache. Qubership’s operator troubleshooting warns that setting cache at or above the pod limit causes OOM kills. This is a container-budgeting pitfall, not an Atlas configuration recipe. (high confidence)
edits.new: Self-managed container sizing must respect the container memory limit and leave room beyond the WiredTiger cache. MongoDB says that when mongod runs in a container without access to all system RAM, the cache size must be set to less than the RAM available in the container, by an amount that depends on the other processes in the container. This is a container-budgeting pitfall, not an Atlas configuration recipe. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/faq/storage/

edits.old: Connection capacity is a separate sizing constraint. Atlas tiers impose connection limits, and per-process application pools can multiply connection demand. A deployment can therefore exhaust connection capacity even when most established connections do little work. (high confidence)
edits.new: Connection capacity is a separate sizing constraint. Atlas tiers impose connection limits, and when an application creates a new MongoClient per request or process, each client can open its own pool up to maxPoolSize, multiplying total open connections. Each connection uses up to 1 megabyte of RAM. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/sizing-tier-selection/ ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/troubleshooting/connection-storms.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/faq/storage/

edits.old: Increasing WiredTiger cache simply because operating-system memory appears available can reduce filesystem caching and worsen disk access. MongoDB advises avoiding increases above the default; Percona describes why starving file buffering can hurt performance. This concerns cache allocation within a fixed RAM budget, not a claim that adding physical RAM is harmful. (high confidence)
edits.new: MongoDB advises avoiding increasing the WiredTiger internal cache size above its default value. MongoDB uses both the WiredTiger internal cache and the operating system's filesystem cache, which uses free memory not taken by the WiredTiger cache and is used by the operating system to reduce disk I/O. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/faq/storage.md
